lesson.title: Bioinformatics: Making Sense of Biology's Big Data
lesson.summary: Bioinformatics uses computational tools and algorithms to organize, compare, and interpret large scale biological data, most often DNA and protein sequences.
lesson.body:
Sequencing a single genome produces an enormous amount of raw data, far too much for any person to sift through by eye. Bioinformatics is the field that grew up to handle this problem, applying computer science and statistics to organize, search, and interpret large scale biological data, especially the DNA sequence data produced by modern sequencing technology.

A lot of bioinformatics work happens before a genome sequence is even usable. Sequencing machines typically read DNA in short fragments called reads, not as one continuous strand, so the first computational task is often assembly, using overlaps between millions of short reads to reconstruct the full, continuous sequence, much like reassembling a jigsaw puzzle from overlapping pieces. Once a sequence is assembled, bioinformatics tools can align it against other sequences, from the same species or different ones, to spot similarities and differences, search enormous public sequence databases for matching or related sequences, and use patterns in the DNA to predict where genes are located and what they might do.

Genomics and bioinformatics are tightly linked, almost inseparable in practice. Genomics is what generates whole genome data in the first place, while bioinformatics is how scientists actually extract meaning from that data. A finished genome sequence on its own is just a long string of letters, it is the computational analysis on top of it, comparing it, searching it, aligning it against other sequences, that turns raw sequence into biological insight.

The applications are wide ranging. Bioinformatics helps identify which genetic variants are associated with disease risk, tracks how a virus mutates as it spreads through a population during an outbreak, and, by systematically comparing DNA sequences across species, helps reconstruct how different organisms are related to one another through evolutionary history, a thread this course picks up directly in the chapters ahead on evolution and natural selection.
